quote: Together they become more optimistic than either would be on their own, each one’s doubts quelled by the other’s seemingly confident reassurance
content: Myers and Lamm's persuasive-arguments theory produces the essay's result once you add the essay's premise. If politeness makes doubts unvoiceable and reassurances free, the pool of arguments aired in discussion leans optimistic, and pooling it moves the group toward optimism. That is polarization toward whatever can be said aloud. The case has been tested directly. People planning a task together predicted they would finish sooner than individuals planning alone, and their discussions dwelt on factors that would help them succeed rather than on obstacles (Buehler, Messervey & Griffin 2005). The essay does not rely on Janis, whose causal chain Fable rightly finds unsupported. "A group of four worriers" would face the same asymmetry: in a room of colleagues, "we can handle it" is the easy thing to say, and "I doubt your competence" is not.

Aviation had to build crew resource management because pilots are not wired to make the distinction the essay calls an artifice. Studies of cockpit communication found first officers "hinting" at dangers in mitigated speech when they needed to state them, and accident investigations traced several crashes to exactly that. The industry's fix was to agree, by training and protocol, that a concern voiced is not an insubordinate disagreement. That is the essay's sentence: "A group of rationalists might agree to pretend there's a difference, but it's not how human beings are really wired." The measured industries proved both halves: the wiring is as the essay said, and an agreed artifice can override it. For pluralistic ignorance, as Fable says, the fix is disclosing the true distribution (Prentice & Miller 1993). One person voicing a concern is that disclosure, carried out one voice at a time.
